extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students of practical politics (early-20th-century New York); readers of political memoir/humor
extracted.subtask_description: Excerpts of a Tammany Hall politician's memoir/practical-advice talks mixing humor, political justification, and policy prescriptions about running a political organization and municipal governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish honest graft from dishonest graft
rubrics_metrics.description: If we bring about some big improvement that benefits the city and it just happens, as a sort of coincidence, that we make a few dollars out of the improvement, they say we are grafters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author defends 'honest graft' as acceptable: listing concrete public works (parks, Washington Bridge, Speedway, Museum of Natural History, viaduct, courthouse) as examples of projects he fathered while also profiting. Implied evaluative rule: profit tied to genuine public benefit is defensible; accusations should be avoided without context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delay moral condemnation—'go slow' before accusing
rubrics_metrics.description: Now, understand; I ain't defendin' the senators who killed the eighty-cent gas bill... I only want to impress the idea to go slow before you make up your mind that a man... has done wrong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance to suspend quick moral judgments about politicians' motives; allow for possibility of honest intent. Used as defense against charges of graft or corruption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political program: New York City should be its own state under Tammany control
rubrics_metrics.description: The time is comm' and though I'm no youngster, I may see it, when New York City will break away from the State and become a state itself... with a Tammany Governor and Legislature... the city would have money to burn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete policy prescriptions tied to this program: extend debt limit in a new constitution to issue more bonds, drop the civil service provisions, enable swift passage of city-sponsored bills, and use passport-like restrictions to limit influx of upstate politicians. Presented as a desirable administrative/financial rubric for municipal development under party control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patriotism measured by ritual, endurance, and public display
rubrics_metrics.description: TAMMANY's the most patriotic organization on earth... The very constitution of the Tammany Society requires that we must assemble at the wigwam on the Fourth... five thousand people, suffocatin' from heat and smoke... yet that crowd stick to their seats... for four solid hours, the Declaration of Independence is read.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines patriotic performance as public ceremony and visible symbols (flags, readings), and endurance of hardship (sitting four hours under heat and big hat). Uses theatrical examples (Grand Sachem wearing stovepipe hat throughout) to argue that visible ritual commitment is the highest patriotism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate patriotism through concrete acts and popular distribution of symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: In 1904 we originated the custom of givin' a small flag to each man as he entered Tammany Hall for the Fourth-of-July celebration... The men waved their flags... The men carried them home and gave them to the children, and the kids got patriotic, too.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocates tangible, populist gestures (flag distribution, offers to raise a regiment) as effective demonstrations of civic devotion and as political investment that spreads loyalty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat political fundraising like legitimate organizational support (akin to church contributions)
rubrics_metrics.description: A political organization has to have money for its business as well as a church... If a corporation sends in a check to help the good work of the Tammany Society, why shouldn't we take it like other missionary societies?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues corporate and personal contributions are proper; candidates are expected to contribute according to their prospective salaries and terms. Explicit norms: contributions are customary, arranged discretely, and are part of reciprocal gratitude to the organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle nominations quietly, avoid public auctioning
rubrics_metrics.description: The man is picked out and somehow he gets to understand what's expected of him in the way of a contribution, and he ponies up—all from gratitude to the organization... When he had his men lined up, he got on a chair... asked for bids... The highest bidder got the nomination for $5000. Now, that wasn't right at all. These things ought to be always fixed up nice and quiet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prescriptive distinction between 'selling' nominations by open auction (condemned) and arranging contributions discretely as custom/expectation (endorsed). Emphasizes decorum and private negotiation as the proper method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Officeholders should reciprocate to the organization (contribute without coercion)
rubrics_metrics.description: As to officeholders, they would be ingrates if they didn't contribute to the organization that put them in office. They needn't be assessed. That would be against the law. But they know what's expected of them...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supports voluntary but normatively expected post-election contributions; recommends polite reminders (anecdote about Dan Donegan's 'shiverin' reminder) rather than force; links civil service protections to decline in such reciprocity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use campaign funds to support district workers and get-out-the-vote efforts
rubrics_metrics.description: Besides the expenses for meetin's, bands and all that, there's the bigger bill for the district workers who get men to the polls... Some of these deservin' citizens have to make enough on registration and election days to keep them the rest of the year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames expenditures on grassroots workers and election-day operatives as legitimate campaign costs and an ethical obligation of the organization to provide livelihoods for these workers.

rubrics_metrics.name: The successful politician does not drink—temperance as a business requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: I HAVE explained how to succeed in politics. I want to add that no matter how well you learn to play the political game, you won't make a lastin' success of it if you're a drinkin' man. I never take a drop... I take for my lieutenants in my district men who don't drink.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treats sobriety as a practical selection criterion for political operatives: drinking leads to unreliability, added costs (guarding drunk employees), and loss of political control. Presents temperance as a pragmatic, not moralistic, rule for personnel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Party bosses are necessary for efficient governance; primary reforms threaten chaos
rubrics_metrics.description: Ignorant people are always talkin' against party bosses, but just wait till the bosses are gone!... Then... will return the good old times, when our district leaders could have nice comfortable primary elections... Who is a better judge of the Democracy of a man... than the leader of the district?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative argument: centralized, experienced party bosses prevent administrative discord and keep the city running smoothly. Prescriptive policy response: repeal primary election law and leave primaries to organizations; leaders should be empowered to vet voters and candidates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oppose punitive excise taxes that impoverish saloonkeepers and create harm
rubrics_metrics.description: The Raines liquor law is infamous. It takes away nearly all the profits of the saloonkeepers... Every time there is an increase of the fee, there is an increase in the suicide record of the city... The Raines law... makes more intemperance and... makes a monopoly in dram shops.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims high license fees and punitive taxation produce unintended harms (suicide, adulterated/poisonous alcohol, monopolies, 'bucket-shops') and penalize small proprietors while favoring sumptuous hotels. Suggests excise policy should protect consumers and small dealers and not merely redistribute to rural/localities. Also argues for differentiated licensing/tax treatment favoring on-premises consumption if necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political messaging should prioritize issues that excite voters; oppose civil service as a political plank
rubrics_metrics.description: The Democratic party... can't die while it's got Tammany for its backbone... The party's got to drop all them put-you-to-sleep issues and come out in 1908 for somethin' that will wake the people up... 'the paramount issue now, always and forever, is the abolition of the iniquitous and villainous civil service laws.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prescription for party platforms: focus on visceral, mobilizing issues rather than abstruse policy disputes; specifically, make abolition of civil service laws the party's leading issue to mobilize support.
